reasoning_traces.think:
The core challenge in cooperative long rope skipping lies in aligning two humanoid agents' whole-body motion with a dynamically evolving rope trajectory. The SE(2) kinematic model ensures that rope turners can translate, rotate, and reposition while maintaining stable contact. This is formalized by defining the rope center \(\mathbf{p}_c\) and rotation axis \(\mathbf{e}_r\) based on base link positions. The hierarchical MARL framework decouples control into low-level decentralized policies and a high-level centralized scheduler. Each agent learns its own manipulation policy through multi-agent reinforcement learning, while the scheduler coordinates their actions. The system must also adapt to diverse player behaviors, which is modeled using a set of jumping policies \(\mathcal{J}\). The loss function \(\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{J})\) captures how well the system generalizes across these styles. Failure modes include loss of synchronization due to phase mismatch, divergence in decentralized policies, or inability to generalize to new player rhythms. These primitives form a dual structure: one for rigid spatial coordination and another for flexible behavioral adaptation.
